subject: Unexpectedly Long Processing Time in GGIR for ActiGraph Data

messages.author: 212ca03e78270775
messages.subject: Unexpectedly Long Processing Time in GGIR for ActiGraph Data
parts:
Hi there,

I am using GGIR to process raw accelerometer data collected from ActiGraph GT3X+ devices. Participants wore the accelerometer for nine days, including continuous wear (day and night) during the seven intermediate full days (midnight to midnight), and removed it on the morning of the ninth day. The data is in CSV format with four columns:
1. HEADER_TIMESTAMP (datetime stamp),
2. X (x-axis acceleration value),
3. Y (y-axis acceleration value), and
4. Z (z-axis acceleration value).

To process the data, I used high-performance computing resources (20 CPUs and 256 GB of RAM). My R version is 4.4.1, and the GGIR version is 3.1.5. However, it takes approximately 17 minutes to process data for one participant, which is significantly longer than the 3–10 minutes mentioned in the tutorial.

For replication purposes, I have attached the following files: the configuration file, R code, and R log ('Experiment_rawacc_log.txt). As the file size exceeds the upload limit, the zipped raw data for one participant has been stored here (https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/pax_g/62161.tar.bz2).

Your suggestions would be greatly appreciated.

Best regards,
Dave

messages.author: 017566be30afa7f3
messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Unexpectedly Long Processing Time in GGIR for ActiGraph Data
parts: which is significantly longer than the 3–10 minutes mentioned in the tutorial.

The time indicated is derived from standard GGIR use cases. Note that you are not processing standard ActiGraph native .gt3x output but a file format specific to one wave of the NHANES study for which I have never tested GGIR. Please understand that without community efforts I do not have the resources to tailor GGIR to every new data format. If accelerometer manufacturers, organisations that collect data, and/or researchers want GGIR to be compatible with new formats then please help coordinate/fund GGIR updates.

That said, with rmc.unit.time = "POSIX" as you are currently using, GGIR will check whether fractions of seconds are missing from the timestamps. This is a rather slow process. Meanwhile rmc.unit.time = "character" does not do this check and assumes that timestamp format is in line with the value of "rmc.format.time" including fractional seconds, so you may want to try that instead as it will run a lot faster.

If this solves your problem then I would appreciate if you could propose:
  • Revisions to the GGIR documentation to make this clear to other users with the same challenge.
  • Expansions to the GGIR documentation to better guide future users of this specific NHANES data format.

Regarding your R script:
I guess your way of appending files is not very memory friendly as it requires that all raw data points from an entire recording fit in memory. Alternatively, you could consider using GGIR parameter maxRecordingInterval https://wadpac.github.io/GGIR/articles/GGIRParameters.html#maxrecordinginterval This will reduce memory needs as data is first processed per file and then appended at feature (metric) level, which avoids that your computer ever needs to hold all raw data in memory at the same time. Further, you could also try a hybrid solution where you may append 2-3 days of raw data and then process it with maxRecordingInterval. Note that all this will affect auto-calibration procedure and by that will cause (minor) inconsistencies in final values.

Thanks,

Vincent

Dr. Vincent van Hees | Independent consultant | https://accelting.com/

messages.subject: Re: [GGIR] Unexpectedly Long Processing Time in GGIR for ActiGraph Data
parts:
Hi Vincent,

Thank you very much for your detailed response. I tried setting rmc.unit.time = "character," which dramatically reduced one participant's processing time from 17 minutes to 5 minutes. However, the output results for sleep onset and offset timings differed significantly between the two settings, which appears not affected by timezone.

Below are the sleep onset and offset timings from the part 5 personal summary file for three participants (left: rmc.unit.time = "POSIX" vs. right: `rmc.unit.time = "character"). The output from "POSIX" appears more reasonable. 


I suspect there might be an issue with the fread() function used by read.myacc.csv. While the data produced by both fread() and vroom() are identical in terms of row count, column count, and column means, I noticed an abnormality when inspecting the first 20 rows of the data using head(data, 20). Specifically, the last row of the output from head(data, 20) displays the header again instead of data, even though head() (default 6 rows) works without any issues. Please find the figures below. When using vroom to read the same data, the abnormality does not appear. Could this behavior of fread() explain the performance issue with GGIR? I have attached the R code. The zipped raw data for one participant has been stored here (https://ftp.cdc.gov/pub/pax_g/62161.tar.bz2).


Thank you very much for your time and kind help!

Best,
Dave
